analysis.one_liner: Phases down US greenhouse gas emissions each year and auctions the right to emit to fund consumer rebates and worker aid.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one House member with zero cosponsors, referred to four committees that took no action, and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a national limit on greenhouse gas pollution, starting with a 5% cut in 2026 and declining by at least 2% of 2005 emissions every year until 2050. The government would sell (auction) a shrinking number of emission permits each quarter, with a $15 minimum price that rises 5% plus inflation annually. Money from the permit sales would fund direct consumer rebates (with a 15% carve-out specifically for low-income rebates), state and local clean-energy programs, funds for communities suffering pollution and for workers displaced by the energy transition, and free permits that gradually phase out for steel, cement, chemical, and other trade-exposed factories. Plants located in designated overburdened communities would face a stricter permit standard, needing a permit for every half ton instead of every ton.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that receive the consumer and low-income rebates; communities with heavy pollution, which get a dedicated fund and a stricter permit standard for nearby plants; workers displaced by the transition to clean energy, who get income and retraining assistance; and clean energy and efficiency industries, which gain customers through state-funded programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, polluted communities, and displaced workers

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in 2026 the bill dedicates 15% of auction proceeds to direct rebates administered by the Treasury, alongside allocations to states that must be used exclusively for consumer energy efficiency, low-emission fuel incentives, or direct financial assistance such as low-income ratepayer relief [S2].

10% of allowances each year are auctioned to fund a Cleaner Air Community Fund, and any stationary source in a designated Cleaner Air Community must surrender a permit for every 0.5 tons it emits instead of one per ton, concentrating cleaner air in overburdened neighborhoods [S2].

The bill directs 5% of allowances each year to a Worker and Community Assistance Fund and creates an Office of Energy and Economic Transition, transition impact studies, assistance for adversely affected workers, and community transition hubs [S2].
All construction projects funded by allowance proceeds must pay locally prevailing wages under Davis-Bacon labor standards [S2].

The bill sets enforceable targets: emissions from covered entities 5% below recent-average levels in 2026, no more than half of 2005 levels by 2030, and no more than 10% of 2005 levels by 2050, with a fallback automatic 3.5% annual cut if the EPA ever fails to set the cap [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, refineries, fossil-fired power plants, heavy industry, and large natural gas utilities pay for emission permits or invest to cut emissions; some of the compliance cost would flow through to consumers as higher fuel and electricity prices, offset by the rebates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, coal, utilities, heavy industry

drawbacks.text: The bill puts a price on every ton of fossil fuel used, so gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity would cost more at the plug or pump before any rebate arrives; whether households come out ahead depends on states delivering their consumer allocations on time and rebate programs keeping pace [S2].

The trading design lets anyone—not just polluters—buy, hold, and sell emission allowances without restriction, which could bring financial speculators into the market and add a layer of middlemen between the climate policy and actual emission cuts [S2].

Energy-intensive, trade-exposed industries like steel and cement receive free allowances for their first ten compliance periods (15% of the cap initially), which shields their costs but reduces auction revenue available for rebates and could hand windfalls to companies whose actual emissions fall faster than their benchmark [S2].

The cost containment reserve can release additional allowances (up to 10% of the reserve) when prices spike, weakening the emissions cap in any given year if polluters choose to pay rather than cut [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a binding, declining national emissions cap with dedicated consumer rebates, low-income protections, pollution relief for overburdened communities, and income support for displaced workers, and its labor standards and phase-down of free industry allocations are stronger than in many cap-and-trade designs. The real risks are price pass-through to households in the years before rebates ramp up and the allowance trading market inviting financial speculation. On the merits it is a serious attempt to cut emissions while protecting the people least able to absorb energy price increases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees, none of which held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the bill on July 30, 2024, near the end of a Congress controlled by a Republican House majority [S1].
No other House member cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor count was zero [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Science, Space, and Technology committees, splitting jurisdiction four ways [S1].

In December 2024 the bill was referred to subcommittees on Work and Welfare and on Trade, a routine step, but no committee or subcommittee took up the bill, and the full action history contains no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal producers, refiners, fossil-fired utilities, and heavy industry are better off: they avoid the permit costs, stricter standards in overburdened communities, and mandatory labor standards the bill would have imposed, while households gain no rebates and polluted communities gain no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy industry

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Climate Pollution Standard and Community Investment Act of 2024 on July 30, 2024.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee, the lead referral for the bill, never held a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling committee calendars and floor scheduling in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor or scheduled action in any of the four committees it was referred to; the bill received zero Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, but the shape was partisan: the sole sponsor was a Democrat, the bill drew zero cosponsors of either party, and a Republican House majority took no action on it.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal producers and refiners
industries.note: Fuel producers and importers would need a permit for every ton their products emit when burned, with the cap declining annually and a triple-penalty for noncompliance. Their costs rise as the cap tightens; the bill's offset is consumer rebates funded by their permit purchases.
Every electricity source of 25 MW or more fired by fossil fuel is a covered entity facing an annually shrinking permit supply, creating a strong incentive to replace plants with renewable generation.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive, trade-exposed manufacturers (steel, cement, chemicals, aluminum)
industries.note: These sectors get free output-based allowances (15% of the cap, phasing out over ten compliance periods) to shield them from foreign competitors, but they still face compliance costs and shrinking assistance, and must eventually pay alongside everyone else.

Large gas utilities must surrender permits for the emissions from gas they deliver to residential and commercial customers, a cost likely to show up in gas bills unless offset by state consumer programs.

industries.industry: Clean energy, efficiency, and clean-tech industries
industries.note: State allocations and state/tribal government proceeds fund efficiency programs, zero-emission generation, storage, EV charging, and manufacturing retooling, creating sustained customer demand as the cap tightens.

Allowances can be freely bought, sold, and banked by anyone, and quarterly public auctions with published clearing prices create a new commodity market; the bill includes purchase limits, beneficial-ownership disclosure, and market oversight to police it.
